title: Deltoid
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 11.5 Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs; 9.6; 8.2; 13.4

main.t: The thick muscle that makes the rounded shape of the shoulder, and the main muscle that lifts the arm sideways.

simpler.t: The deltoid is your shoulder muscle. It lifts your arm out to the side.

deeper.t: It is the major abductor of the arm, and it also helps to flex, extend and rotate it.

facts.t: The deltoid caps the shoulder joint, covering it from the front, the side and the back.
Its fibres arise from the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula.
It inserts on the deltoid tuberosity, about halfway down the outer side of the humerus.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The deltoid’s insertion (deltoid tuberosity of the humerus).

simpler.t: It wraps over the top of your shoulder, from your collarbone and shoulder blade to your upper arm bone.

deeper.t: Its origin follows the insertion of the trapezius on the clavicle, acromion and scapular spine.

items.name: Clavicular (front) part
items.t: Arises from the clavicle. It helps flex and medially rotate the arm.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Which parts of the deltoid flex and which extend the arm (OpenStax names the actions, not the parts).

items.name: Acromial (middle) part
items.t: Arises from the acromion. It is the part that abducts the arm.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). That the middle (acromial) fibres are the ones that abduct.

items.name: Spinal (back) part
items.t: Arises from the spine of the scapula. It helps extend and laterally rotate the arm.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Which parts of the deltoid flex and which extend the arm (OpenStax names the actions, not the parts).

items.name: Shape
items.t: Thick and triangular, like the Greek letter delta, which gives it its name.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The origin of the name (the Greek letter delta).

simpler.t: It has a front, a middle and a back part, all meeting on the upper arm.

deeper.t: Its front and back parts work against each other, so the deltoid can both flex and extend the arm.
deeper.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Which parts of the deltoid flex and which extend the arm (OpenStax names the actions, not the parts).

facts.t: Its fibres arch over the shoulder, so pulling on the humerus lifts the arm away from the body.
The front fibres flex and medially rotate the arm. The back fibres extend and laterally rotate it.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Which parts of the deltoid flex and which extend the arm (OpenStax names the actions, not the parts).

facts.t: Its thickness gives the shoulder its rounded outline.

simpler.t: Because it sits over the top of the shoulder, it lifts the arm out to the side.

items.name: Supraspinatus
items.t: A rotator cuff muscle deep to the deltoid. It also abducts the arm.

items.name: Glenohumeral (shoulder) joint
items.t: The deltoid covers this joint, formed by the humeral head and the glenoid cavity.

items.name: Trapezius
items.t: Attaches to the same line of clavicle, acromion and scapular spine, from above.

items.name: Pectoralis major
items.t: The axial muscle in front. It shares the job of bringing the arm forwards.

items.name: Axillary nerve
items.t: A branch of the radial nerve that goes to the armpit region. It supplies the deltoid.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). That the axillary nerve supplies the deltoid.

simpler.t: It covers the shoulder joint, with the rotator cuff underneath and the trapezius above.

facts.t: Like other limb muscles, it develops from general mesoderm rather than from somites.
Its fibres form when many myoblasts fuse, which is why each fibre has many nuclei.
Training adds structural proteins to its fibres, so the muscle grows thicker without adding fibres.

items.injury: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus after a fall.
items.damaged: The axillary nerve, which winds round the surgical neck to reach the deltoid.
items.cannotDo: Lift the arm out to the side with normal strength.
items.why: Without its nerve, the deltoid cannot contract, so abduction is weak.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The course of the axillary nerve round the surgical neck, and the weakness that follows its injury.

items.injury: A shoulder kept still for weeks after an injury.
items.cannotDo: Lift the arm with the strength they had before.
items.why: Unused muscle loses structural proteins and shrinks (disuse atrophy).

items.q: Explain how one muscle, the deltoid, can both flex and extend the arm.
model: The deltoid has front, middle and back parts.
The front part lies in front of the joint and flexes the arm.
The back part lies behind the joint and extends it.
So its parts can act as antagonists to each other.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Which parts of the deltoid flex and which extend the arm (OpenStax names the actions, not the parts).

items.q: Compare the deltoid and the supraspinatus in abducting the arm.
model: The deltoid is the major abductor and lies superficially, capping the shoulder.
The supraspinatus lies deep, above the spine of the scapula.
Its tendon is part of the rotator cuff, which steadies the joint.

items.q: Predict what a patient cannot do after a fracture of the surgical neck that injures the axillary nerve.
model: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid.
The deltoid cannot contract without it.
Abduction of the arm becomes weak.
Over time the unused muscle wastes, flattening the shoulder’s outline.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The axillary nerve’s supply to the deltoid and the signs of its injury.

check.stem: Which movement is the deltoid’s main action?
check.why: The deltoid is the major abductor of the arm.

check.stem: Which of these is not an origin of the deltoid?
check.why: The deltoid arises from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula. The coracoid process gives origin to the coracobrachialis.

check.stem: What gives the shoulder its rounded outline?
options: The head of the humerus alone
check.why: The thick deltoid creates the rounded lines of the shoulder.
